intro: Welcome to your Robotics & AI adventure! 🤖 Work through the lessons in order. Read the notes, watch the videos, look at the pictures, try the activities — then take the lesson quiz to earn XP. You learn best by doing, so have fun and don't be afraid to experiment!

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Robotics & AI Basics
lessons.summary: What is a robot? What is AI? Where do we see them in real life?

notes.text: A robot is a machine that can sense the world around it, think about what to do, and then act — like moving, beeping, or lighting up. Robots do jobs that are boring, dangerous, or very precise.

notes.title: What is a robot? What is AI?

notes.text:
Every robot has three main parts:
👀 Sensors — to feel the world (like eyes and ears).
🧠 A controller (brain) — to make decisions.
🦿 Actuators — motors and lights that make it move or react.

AI (Artificial Intelligence) is when a computer learns to do clever things — like recognising a face, understanding speech, or spotting a cat in a photo. Just like you get better with practice, AI gets better by looking at lots of examples.

🌍 Real-world robots & AI: factory arms building cars, robot vacuum cleaners, self-driving cars, drones, voice assistants like Siri, and robots that explore Mars! In the future, robots will help even more in hospitals, farms, and homes.
🔎 Try it! Look around your home. Can you spot 3 machines that 'sense' something and react? (Hint: a fridge light, an automatic door, a phone that unlocks with your face.)

quiz.question: What are the three main jobs every robot does?
quiz.explanation: Every robot senses the world, thinks about what to do, then acts — that's the heart of robotics!

quiz.question: AI gets better by looking at lots of examples, just like you get better with practice.
quiz.explanation: Exactly right — the more good examples an AI sees, the smarter it gets.

quiz.question: The part of a robot that works like its brain and makes decisions is called the ______.
quiz.explanation: The controller (brain) takes information from the sensors and decides what to do.

quiz.question: Match each robot part to its job.
quiz.explanation: Sensors feel, the controller thinks, and actuators act — sense, think, act!

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Arduino & Electronics
lessons.summary: Meet the Arduino board and the basic electronic parts.

notes.text: Arduino is a tiny computer board that acts as a robot's brain. You give it instructions (a program), and it controls lights, motors, and reads sensors.

🧰 Basic electronic parts you'll use:
• Resistor — slows down electricity to protect parts.
• LED — a small light 💡.
• Buzzer — makes sound 🔊.
• Capacitor — stores a little electricity.
• Diode — lets electricity flow one way only.
• DC motor — spins to make things move.
• Switch — turns a circuit on or off.
Electricity needs a complete loop called a circuit. If the loop is broken (like a switch turned off), nothing works — just like water can't flow through a cut pipe.
A breadboard lets you build circuits by pushing parts into holes — no glue or soldering needed. Perfect for trying ideas and fixing mistakes quickly!

💡 Try it! On a breadboard, light one LED using a battery and a resistor. Then add a switch so you can turn it on and off. What happens if you remove the resistor? (Ask your teacher — never skip it, it protects the LED!)

quiz.question: What does a resistor do in a circuit?
options: Slows down electricity to protect parts
quiz.answer: Slows down electricity to protect parts
quiz.explanation: A resistor limits the current so delicate parts like LEDs don't get too much electricity and burn out.

quiz.question: Electricity needs a complete loop (a circuit) to flow.
quiz.explanation: If the loop is broken anywhere, the electricity can't flow — just like water in a cut pipe.

quiz.question: A board you push parts into to build circuits without soldering is called a ______.
quiz.explanation: A breadboard lets you build and change circuits quickly — perfect for experimenting.

quiz.question: Match each component to what it does.

pairs.match: Turns a circuit on or off

quiz.explanation: Each component has one clear job — mixing them lets you build amazing things!

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — micro:bit Coding
lessons.summary: Program the micro:bit with easy drag-and-drop blocks.

notes.text: The micro:bit is a pocket-sized computer with 25 tiny LEDs, 2 buttons (A and B), and built-in sensors. It's a super friendly way to start coding.
You program it with blocks — colourful puzzle pieces you drag together. No typing needed at first! Later you can switch to text code when you're ready.

💡 Inputs are things the micro:bit senses: button presses, shaking, light, and temperature.
🔆 Outputs are things it does: light up LEDs, show pictures, or make sounds.
A simple idea: WHEN button A is pressed → SHOW a heart ❤️. That's input → action, the same 'sense and act' idea from Lesson 1!
🎮 Try it! In the micro:bit editor, make a program: when you press button A, show a smiley 😀; when you press button B, show a heart ❤️. Then try 'on shake → show a random number' to build a dice!

quiz.question: How many tiny LEDs are on the front of a micro:bit?
quiz.explanation: The micro:bit has a 5×5 grid of LEDs — that's 25 lights you can control!

quiz.question: You can program the micro:bit by dragging colourful blocks together, with no typing at first.
quiz.explanation: Blocks are like puzzle pieces — a friendly way to start before moving to text code.

quiz.question: Pressing button A is an example of an ______ — something the micro:bit senses.
quiz.explanation: Inputs are things the micro:bit senses; outputs are things it does.

quiz.question: Is each one an input or an output?
quiz.explanation: Sensing = input, doing = output. It's the sense-and-act idea again!

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Arduino Programming
lessons.summary: Write code for the Arduino using the Arduino IDE and Tinkercad.

notes.text: We write Arduino programs in the Arduino IDE (a free app) and can test them for free online in Tinkercad before using real parts.

notes.title: Your first Arduino program (blink an LED)

notes.text:
Every Arduino program has two main parts:
• setup() — runs once at the start (get things ready).
• loop() — runs again and again forever (the robot's heartbeat).

🧱 Building blocks of code:
• Variables store information (like a labelled box).
• Loops repeat actions.
• Conditionals (if / else) make decisions: IF it's dark → turn the light ON.

Arduino pins can be INPUT (read a sensor) or OUTPUT (control an LED or motor). The Serial Monitor lets the Arduino print messages to your screen — great for checking what's happening and fixing bugs 🐞.
✨ Try it! In Tinkercad, make an LED blink: turn it ON, wait 1 second, turn it OFF, wait 1 second — forever. Change the waiting time to make it blink faster or slower!

quiz.question: Which part of an Arduino program runs again and again, forever?
quiz.explanation: loop() is the robot's heartbeat — it repeats forever. setup() runs just once at the start.

quiz.question: setup() runs only once, at the very start of the program.
quiz.explanation: setup() gets everything ready one time; then loop() takes over and repeats.

quiz.question: The ______ Monitor lets the Arduino print messages to your screen to help you find bugs.
quiz.explanation: The Serial Monitor is a coder's best friend for seeing what the Arduino is thinking.

quiz.question: Match each code building-block to its job.
quiz.explanation: Variables remember, loops repeat, and conditionals decide — the basics of all code!

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Sensors & Actuators
lessons.summary: How robots feel the world and how they move.

notes.text:
Sensors are the robot's senses (inputs). Some common ones:
• Ultrasonic — measures distance with sound 🔊.
• IR — spots objects or follows a line.
• LDR — senses light (bright or dark).
• Temperature — senses hot or cold.
• Touch / limit — senses a press or bump.

Actuators make the robot do things (outputs):
• DC motor — spins wheels to drive around.
• Servo motor — turns to an exact angle (great for arms and steering).
• LED & buzzer — light and sound to show what's happening.
The magic is putting them together: a sensor gives the Arduino information, the Arduino decides, and an actuator acts. This is called feedback control.
🎯 Try it! Idea for a mini-project: use an ultrasonic sensor so a buzzer beeps faster as your hand gets closer — like a car parking sensor! Or use an LDR to turn on an LED when it gets dark.

quiz.question: Which sensor measures distance using sound waves?
quiz.explanation: An ultrasonic sensor sends a sound, times the echo coming back, and works out the distance.

quiz.question: A servo motor can turn to an exact angle, which is great for robot arms and steering.
quiz.explanation: Servos 'aim' to a position (0°–180°), while DC motors just 'spin'.

quiz.question: An ______ sensor (also called an LDR) senses whether it is bright or dark.
quiz.explanation: An LDR — Light Dependent Resistor — changes with how much light hits it.

quiz.question: Match each part to what it does.
quiz.explanation: Sensors feel; actuators act. Together they make feedback control!

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — AI & Machine Learning
lessons.summary: Teach a computer to recognise pictures, sounds, and poses.

notes.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a type of AI where a computer learns from examples instead of being told every rule. Show it lots of cat photos and dog photos, and it learns to tell them apart!

notes.title: Teach a machine with Google Teachable Machine

notes.text:
The steps are always the same:
1️⃣ Collect examples (photos, sounds, or poses).
2️⃣ Train the model on those examples.
3️⃣ Predict — show it something new and it guesses the answer.
Google Teachable Machine is a free website 🌐 that lets you train your own AI in minutes — right in your browser. You can teach it to recognise images, sounds, or body poses.
⚖️ Important: AI is only as good as its examples. If you give it messy or unfair examples, it makes mistakes. Good examples = smart AI!
📷 Try it! On Teachable Machine, train an image model with two classes: 'thumbs up 👍' and 'thumbs down 👎'. Give lots of examples of each, then test it live with your webcam. How accurate is it?

quiz.question: In machine learning, how does a computer learn to do a task?
options: By being told every single rule
quiz.explanation: Instead of writing every rule, we show the computer many examples and it finds the patterns.

quiz.question: AI is only as good as the examples you give it — messy examples lead to mistakes.
quiz.explanation: Good, fair examples make a smart AI. Rubbish in, rubbish out!

quiz.question: A free website that lets you train your own AI in the browser is Google ______ Machine.
quiz.explanation: Google Teachable Machine trains image, sound, or pose models in minutes.

quiz.question: Put the three ML steps in order by matching them to what happens.

pairs.match: Guess the answer for something new

quiz.explanation: Collect → Train → Predict. That's the machine-learning recipe!

lessons.title: Lesson 7 — Build a Robot
lessons.summary: Design, build, and program an obstacle-avoidance robot.

notes.text: Now we bring everything together to build an obstacle-avoidance robot — a robot car that drives around and turns away when it sees something in the way.

🛠️ The build steps:
1️⃣ Build the body (chassis) and attach the wheels and motors.
2️⃣ Add the Arduino brain and the battery.
3️⃣ Fit an ultrasonic sensor at the front (the robot's eyes 👀).
4️⃣ Upload the code.
5️⃣ Test and improve!

🧠 The robot's thinking (the code idea):
IF something is close in front → STOP and turn.
ELSE → drive forward.
This repeats over and over in the loop(), just like Lesson 4.
🧪 Testing & refining means trying it, seeing what goes wrong, and fixing it — maybe the turn is too small, or it stops too late. Real engineers improve their robots this way!
📓 Try it! Keep a project logbook. Draw your robot, list its parts, and write down every problem you fixed. What distance should trigger a turn — 10 cm or 20 cm? Test both and pick the best!

quiz.question: What does an obstacle-avoidance robot do when something is close in front of it?
quiz.explanation: IF something is close → STOP and turn; ELSE → drive forward. That simple rule keeps it out of trouble!

quiz.question: The robot's thinking code repeats over and over inside the loop().
quiz.explanation: Checking the sensor and deciding happens again and again in loop() — the robot's heartbeat.

quiz.question: The front sensor that acts as the robot's 'eyes' is the ______ sensor.
quiz.explanation: The ultrasonic sensor measures how far away things are, so the robot can avoid them.

quiz.question: Match each robot part to its role.
quiz.explanation: Body, eyes, brain, and power — put them together and your robot comes alive!

lessons.title: Lesson 8 — Project & Future
lessons.summary: Show off your robot and dream about what's next!

notes.text: 🎉 Project Showcase! This is where you show your robot to others, explain how it works, and maybe race it in a friendly competition. Be proud — you built a real robot!
📝 Your project report tells the story of your robot: your design idea, how you coded it, the problems you faced, and what you learned from start to finish.

🔮 The future of robotics: robots that help doctors, farm our food, clean the oceans, and explore space. AI is getting smarter every year. The skills you learned here — sensing, thinking, acting, and coding — are the same ones real engineers use!
🌟 Try it! Imagine a robot that solves a problem in YOUR life. What does it sense? What does it do? Draw it and give it a name. Who knows — you might build it one day!

quiz.question: What four key skills did you practise all through this course?
quiz.explanation: Sense, think, act, and code — the very same skills real robotics engineers use!

quiz.question: A project report tells the story of how you designed, built, and improved your robot.
quiz.explanation: It captures your idea, your code, the problems you solved, and what you learned.

quiz.question: Trying your robot, seeing what goes wrong, and fixing it is called ______ and refining.
quiz.explanation: Testing and refining is how every engineer turns a good robot into a great one.

quiz.question: Match each place to how robots might help there in the future.
quiz.explanation: Robots and AI will help everywhere — and you now know how they work!

lessons.title: L298N Motor Driver
lessons.summary: Meet the chip that makes robot cars move — parts, direction, speed, wiring, and code.

steps.title: Meet the L298N
steps.text: This whole robot car is controlled by ONE tiny black chip. Today, YOU become the person who understands it better than anyone in the room. Let's go! 🚀

steps.question: Before we start — have you ever seen a little robot car that drives by itself?
options: Never, but I want to build one! 🔧
steps.title: Warm-up
steps.reaction: Awesome — by the end of this you'll know how it MOVES! 🚗

steps.title: Why do motors even need a 'driver'?

blocks.text: An Arduino is a great little brain — but it's weak. Each pin can only push about 20mA of current. That's tiny!
A DC motor is hungry — it needs hundreds of milliamps, sometimes whole Amps, to spin.
So we put the L298N in the middle. The Arduino whispers small orders, and the L298N supplies the big muscle to actually turn the motors.
Think of it like this: Arduino = the brain giving orders. L298N = the bodyguard who does the heavy lifting.

steps.title: Here it is — in 3D!
steps.text: This is a real L298N module. Grab it with your mouse (or finger) and spin it around. Look at the big chip, the silver fins, and all those pins.

blocks.caption: Drag to spin the real L298N in 3D!

steps.title: The real board — up close 📸
steps.text: Here's an actual L298N module, seen from the top. Look for the black heatsink on top, the two tall capacitors, the blue motor terminals on the left & right, and the power terminal + IN pins along the bottom.

blocks.alt: A real L298N motor driver module, top view
blocks.caption: A real L298N module — the parts you'll name next.

steps.title: The anatomy — top of the board

blocks.text: The black chip (IC) in the middle is the real L298N — it secretly holds two motor controllers, so one board can drive 2 motors.
The silver fins on top are the heatsink. Motors pull lots of current, current makes heat, and the heatsink keeps the chip cool. 🧊
The blue screw block up top is the power terminal: 12V (motor power in), GND (ground), and 5V.
OUT1 / OUT2 → wires to Motor A.   OUT3 / OUT4 → wires to Motor B.
IN1, IN2 decide the direction of Motor A. IN3, IN4 do the same for Motor B.
ENA and ENB are the speed / on-off pins for each motor.
The little yellow 5V jumper lets the board make its own 5V from the 12V input — handy for powering the Arduino.
Remember two jobs: IN pins = which way, EN pins = how fast.

steps.title: Grab your board!
steps.html: Hands-on: Pick up your real L298N module. Point to the big black chip, the silver heatsink, and the blue screw terminals. Show your neighbour the OUT1/OUT2 side (Motor A).
steps.hint: No kit today? No problem — spin the 3D model above instead and point at each part on screen.

steps.title: Game 1 — Label the Board
steps.text: A part lights up with a red flag. Tap its correct name. 3 lives — how many can you get?

steps.title: Quiz 1 · Q1
steps.question: What is the heatsink's job?
steps.explain: Current makes heat, and the heatsink's fins carry that heat away so the chip stays safe.

steps.title: Quiz 1 · Q2
steps.question: How many motors can ONE L298N module control at once?
steps.explain: The chip has two H-Bridges inside — one for Motor A, one for Motor B.

steps.title: Quiz 1 · Q3
steps.question: Which pins decide a motor's DIRECTION?
steps.explain: IN pins = direction. (ENA/ENB are for speed.)

steps.title: Quiz 1 · Q4
steps.question: Which pin controls a motor's SPEED?
steps.explain: ENA/ENB set the speed using PWM (a value from 0 to 255).

steps.title: Badge unlocked: Board Namer!
steps.text: You can now name every part of the L298N. Next up: how it flips a motor's direction like magic. Tap Next for Session 2! ➡️

steps.title: Session 2 — The Traffic Cop
steps.text: The L298N is like a traffic cop for electricity: it decides which way the current flows through your motor. Let's see the trick inside.

blocks.text: A motor spins one way when current flows through it in one direction — and the opposite way when you reverse the current.
Inside the chip are 4 switches arranged in the shape of an H, with the motor in the middle. Flip different switches and the current changes direction — without ever swapping the wires!
IN1 and IN2 are your remote control for those switches. That's the whole secret. 🪄

steps.title: The Truth Table — the heart of it all

blocks.text: Here's exactly what Motor A does for each combination of IN1 and IN2:
• IN1 = LOW, IN2 = LOW → motor coasts (free stop) ⏸️
• IN1 = HIGH, IN2 = LOW → FORWARD ➡️
• IN1 = LOW, IN2 = HIGH → BACKWARD ⬅️
• IN1 = HIGH, IN2 = HIGH → BRAKE (hard stop) 🛑
Same LOW → stop-ish. Different → spin. Both HIGH → brake. Try it yourself next! 👇

steps.title: Game 2 — Traffic Cop Simulator
steps.text: You are the traffic cop! Flip IN1 and IN2 and slide the speed. Watch the motor react. Can you make it brake?

blocks.text: The IN pins pick the direction. The ENA (and ENB) pin picks the speed.
• ENA = 0 → motor OFF (no matter what IN1/IN2 say)
• ENA = 255 → full speed
• ENA = anything in between → that % of speed. This is called PWM.

steps.title: Game 3 — Predict the Motor
steps.text: Quiz-show time! Read IN1 and IN2, then tap Forward / Backward / Stop / Brake before the timer runs out. Streak bonus for combos! 🔥

steps.title: Quiz 2 · Q1
steps.question: If IN1 = HIGH and IN2 = HIGH, what happens?
steps.explain: Both HIGH tells the H-Bridge to lock the motor — a hard brake.

steps.title: Quiz 2 · Q2
steps.question: What controls the motor's SPEED (not direction)?
steps.explain: PWM on ENA/ENB (0–255) sets how fast; IN pins only set direction.

steps.title: Quiz 2 · Q3
steps.question: If ENA = LOW, what happens even if IN1 = HIGH and IN2 = LOW?
steps.explain: ENA is the master switch. If it's LOW, the motor can't run — direction doesn't matter.

steps.title: Badge unlocked: Traffic Cop!
steps.text: You've mastered direction and speed. Now let's wire the whole thing together. On to Session 3! ➡️

steps.title: Session 3 — Wire It Up
steps.text: Time to connect everything: Arduino, L298N, battery, and two motors. Follow the map and watch out for the #1 beginner trap!

blocks.text: 12V → + of the battery pack (7–12V).   GND → – of the battery.
IN1, IN2, IN3, IN4 → Arduino digital pins (e.g. D8, D9, D10, D11).
ENA, ENB → Arduino PWM pins (e.g. D5, D6) for speed.
OUT1/OUT2 → Motor A.   OUT3/OUT4 → Motor B.
Every ground must meet every other ground. The battery's GND, the L298N's GND, and the Arduino's GND must ALL connect together.
This shared ground is the #1 mistake beginners make. If the motors act crazy or dead, check the ground first!
Say it with me three times: every ground must meet every other ground. 🤝

steps.title: Find the ground!
steps.html: Hands-on: On your board, find the middle screw of the power terminal — that's GND. Trace where it needs to go: to the battery's – AND to the Arduino's GND pin.
steps.hint: No kit? Point to GND on the wiring map above and say out loud where the two ground wires go.

steps.title: Quiz 3 · Q1
steps.question: Why must the Arduino GND and the battery GND be connected together?
options: So they share a common reference — signals work
steps.answer: So they share a common reference — signals work
steps.explain: Without a shared ground, the Arduino's HIGH/LOW signals mean nothing to the L298N.

steps.title: Quiz 3 · Q2
steps.question: Which pin would you NEVER plug a motor into?
steps.explain: Motors go on the OUT pins. IN1 is a tiny logic signal pin — a motor there won't work (and could cause trouble).

steps.title: Quiz 3 · Q3
steps.question: Spot the bug: a robot's motors do nothing. Arduino code is fine. What's the most likely problem?
options: The chip is upside down inside
steps.explain: No common ground = no working signals. Always check ground first!

steps.title: Badge unlocked: Certified Wirer!
steps.text: Your circuit is solid. Last stop: telling the L298N what to do with real code. Session 4! ➡️

steps.title: Session 4 — Speak Its Language
steps.text: Everything you learned maps straight onto real Arduino code. Watch how each line is just something you already know!

blocks.title: motor_demo.ino

blocks.text: pinMode(..., OUTPUT) = "Arduino, get ready to send orders on this pin."
digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH/LOW) = flipping a switch → this is your Session 2 truth table!
analogWrite(ENA, 0–255) = the speed dial (PWM).
delay(2000) = hold that state for 2000 ms (2 seconds).

steps.title: Quiz 4 · Q1
steps.question: In code, digitalWrite(IN1, HIGH); digitalWrite(IN2, LOW); makes the motor…
steps.explain: HIGH/LOW on IN1/IN2 = forward, exactly like the truth table.

steps.title: Quiz 4 · Q2
steps.question: Which line sets the SPEED?
steps.explain: analogWrite on the EN pin = PWM speed (0–255).

steps.title: Game 4 — Build-a-Sequence
steps.text: Drag blocks to program your virtual car, then hit Run! Complete the challenge to earn your final badge.
steps.challenge: Make the car go forward, then reverse, then stop.

steps.title: L298N Certified!
steps.text: You did it! You can name the board, control direction and speed, wire it safely, and read the code. You're officially an L298N driver. 🌟

quiz.question: How many motors can one L298N drive?
IN1 and IN2 control the motor's SPEED.
IN1=LOW, IN2=HIGH means the motor…
The #1 beginner wiring mistake is…
The function that sets PWM speed on ENA is analog____(ENA, 200).

lessons.title: Obstacle-Avoidance Robot — Day 2: Wire the Motors
lessons.summary: Connect your two DC motors and battery pack to the L298N motor driver on the chassis you built last class, and watch the wheels spin!

steps.title: Welcome back — Day 2!
steps.text: Last class you built your robot's body. Today we give it muscles! By the end of today, your wheels will actually spin. 🚀

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.question: Do you remember what the L298N motor driver does?
options: Yes — it's the muscle that powers the motors! 💪
Not really, but I'm ready to learn! 🔌
steps.reaction: The Arduino can't power motors directly — it sends tiny signals, and the L298N supplies the real muscle. Let's put that to work!

blocks.text: The Arduino is the brain — it sends small signals. The L298N is the muscle — it takes battery power and drives the motors. Today we wire that muscle onto your chassis.

items.name: Your Chassis
items.text: The body you built last class — motors, wheels, caster and battery holder already mounted.

items.name: Motor Driver (L298N)
items.text: Bolts onto your chassis and connects to both motors and the battery.

items.name: Jumper Wires
items.text: Connect the motors and battery to the driver — no soldering needed.

items.name: 3.7V Batteries ×2
items.text: Already in your battery holder — today we connect them to the driver.

blocks.text: No Arduino code today — that's Day 4! Today is 100% hands-on wiring.

steps.title: Grab your Day 1 chassis!
steps.html: Hands-on: Get your chassis, L298N driver, jumper wires and the L298N handout from last class. Sit with the same team.
steps.hint: Chassis wheel loose? Tighten its screw before we start wiring.

blocks.title: Wiring the motors and motor driver

blocks.text: Watch the whole clip once together, then replay it while your team wires — pause anytime you need to catch up!
Each motor connects to one pair of OUT terminals: OUT1/OUT2 for the left motor, OUT3/OUT4 for the right motor. The battery pack connects to the driver's power terminal.
The Golden Rule: every ground (GND) wire must connect back to the same shared ground. Skip this and nothing will work!

steps.title: Wire it up!
steps.html: Hands-on: With your team — 1) Left motor wires → OUT1/OUT2. 2) Right motor wires → OUT3/OUT4. 3) Battery pack → the power terminal (watch + and −!). 4) Double-check the shared ground. Show your teacher before connecting power.
steps.hint: Wheels spinning backwards? Just swap that motor's two wires at the OUT terminal.

steps.title: Quick check · Q1
steps.question: Which OUT terminals does the left motor connect to?
steps.explain: OUT1/OUT2 is Motor A's pair of terminals — that's where the left motor's two wires connect.

steps.title: Quick check · Q2
steps.question: What happens on Day 3 of the build?
steps.explain: Day 3 gives your robot 'eyes' — the ultrasonic sensor that lets it detect obstacles.

steps.title: Your wheels are spinning!
steps.text: Fantastic work — your robot has muscles now! Next class (Day 3) we add the ultrasonic sensor so it can 'see' obstacles. 🚀

quiz.question: What does the L298N motor driver do?
options: Takes battery power and drives the motors
quiz.answer: Takes battery power and drives the motors
quiz.explanation: The Arduino only sends small control signals — the L298N supplies the real power that spins the motors.

quiz.question: Every ground (GND) wire in the circuit must connect back to the same shared ground.
quiz.explanation: A shared ground completes the circuit for every part — without it, signals and power don't have a return path and nothing works.

quiz.question: If a motor spins the wrong way, what's the easiest fix?
options: Swap that motor's two wires at the OUT terminal
quiz.answer: Swap that motor's two wires at the OUT terminal
quiz.explanation: Reversing the two wires at the OUT terminal reverses that motor's spin direction — a quick fix with no code needed.

quiz.question: The right motor connects to the OUT3 / OUT____ terminals.
quiz.explanation: OUT3 and OUT4 form Motor B's pair of terminals on the L298N.
